entries.title: Mulberry may reshape gut bacteria and influence metabolism
entries.summary: Mulberry compounds may reshape the gut microbiome in ways that support intestinal health and metabolism, with some combinations showing especially strong effects in animal studies. However, the results vary depending on the plant part and processing method, and the benefits have yet to be confirmed

entries.title: Bats may have first evolved in Europe 65 million years ago
entries.summary: A huge genomic and fossil study suggests bats first evolved in Europe around 65 to 60 million years ago before spreading across the globe. The findings also indicate that flight and echolocation emerged near the beginning of bat evolution, potentially helping explain how bats became one of the most

entries.title: A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
entries.summary: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. entries.title: These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
entries.summary: Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as

entries.title: A 240-million-year-old fossil just changed the dinosaur timeline
entries.summary: A newly identified 240-million-year-old animal from Tanzania is forcing scientists to rethink the early dinosaur timeline. entries.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
entries.summary: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosa

entries.title: Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
entries.summary: Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. entries.title: Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
entries.summary: A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. entries.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
entries.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. entries.title: This 245-million-year-old fossil still has its stomach and intestines
entries.summary: A 245-million-year-old marine reptile fossil preserves an astonishing amount of detail, including its stomach, liver, and intestines. The discovery reveals that Austronaga minuta was highly adapted for swimming even though its digestive system remained surprisingly simple.

entries.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
entries.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with rese

entries.title: Scientists discover a bizarre Jurassic “squid” unlike anything ever seen
entries.summary: Scientists have identified the “fattest” belemnite ever discovered, a bizarre, barrel-shaped squid relative that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago. The exceptionally rare fossils reveal a creature unlike anything previously known, potentially a predator of smaller squid-like anim

entries.title: UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile
entries.summary: A 125-million-year-old crocodile fossil has revealed preserved skin, possible sensory organs, sophisticated respiratory structures, and an unexpected pattern on its tail. Ultraviolet light exposed alternating bands that may represent ancient camouflage, potentially preserving the oldest known colora

entries.title: 210-million-year-old dinosaur discovery reveals a lost world in Africa
entries.summary: A newly identified 210-million-year-old dinosaur from Zimbabwe is helping scientists uncover a surprisingly distinct prehistoric ecosystem. The discovery suggests that ancient climate differences may have separated dinosaur populations across southern Africa, leading to unique species that challenge

entries.title: This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
entries.summary: A 165-million-year-old fossil has revealed an extraordinary Jurassic predator that may help explain how mammals developed one of their most important evolutionary advantages. Although only 20 inches long, Megacauda sungei was a heavyweight among early mammal relatives, swimming through ancient water

entries.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
entries.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help expl

entries.title: A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
entries.summary: Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.

entries.title: Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
entries.summary: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such

entries.title: Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
entries.summary: New research suggests animals could have evolved as early as 800 to 700 million years ago, roughly 200 million years earlier than some previous estimates. If so, the first animals may have lived before or during Snowball Earth, leaving behind little trace because their soft bodies were rarely preser

entries.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
entries.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

entries.title: Scientists discover a mysterious new frog hiding in the Amazon
entries.summary: Scientists discovered a new frog species in the flooded forests of the western Amazon, distinguishing it from nearly identical relatives through DNA and its unique call. entries.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
entries.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.

entries.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
entries.summary: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. entries.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
entries.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise

entries.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
entries.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. entries.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
entries.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. entries.title: This giant stick insect fooled scientists for decades
entries.summary: Scientists have identified two new species of large Australian stick insects, including one that lays extraordinary “lidded” eggs never before recorded in the group. The discovery also revealed that a familiar stick insect had been misidentified for decades, showing how much biodiversity may still b

entries.title: New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
entries.summary: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

entries.title: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
entries.summary: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simple

entries.title: Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
entries.summary: Cats may identify one another through a surprisingly durable chemical “calling card” made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. The compounds appear linked to mysterious fat droplets in the kidneys and may represent a scent-recognition system shared across the cat family.

entries.title: NASA-backed scientists turn plastic waste into edible cookies
entries.summary: Scientists have engineered yeast to turn PET plastic and agricultural waste into ingredients for protein-rich, 3D-printed cookies called µBites. Developed partly for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge, the system can produce proteins, fats, vitamins, and even vanilla flavoring from waste materials. Re

entries.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
entries.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. entries.title: The “glue” holding your cells together has a surprising second job
entries.summary: Scientists have discovered that E-cadherin, a protein best known as the “glue” holding cells and tissues together, has a surprising second job: helping epithelial cells swallow nearby dead cells. entries.title: Scientists say house cats could help unlock better cancer treatments for humans
entries.summary: Scientists have mapped the genetics of cat cancer on an unprecedented scale and found surprising similarities with tumors in humans. The findings could help bring precision cancer treatments to cats while also revealing new clues about how human cancers develop and respond to drugs.

entries.title: New chemical wipes out 95% of termites without harming humans
entries.summary: A chemical that stops drywood termites from building new exoskeletons killed about 95% of colonies in testing, offering a potentially safer alternative to traditional fumigation. Because termites eventually have no choice but to molt, the treatment turns a normal stage of their life cycle into a fat

entries.title: This tiny organism can shrink to one quarter its size in milliseconds
entries.summary: A single-celled organism can shrink to one-quarter of its length in milliseconds using a remarkable calcium-powered protein “fishnet.” Scientists hope its unusual machinery could inspire artificial muscles capable of moving far faster than today’s designs.

entries.title: Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
entries.summary: Archaeologists have discovered 1,200-year-old remains of Peru’s famous hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site, including remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans. Their unusual teeth, diets, and burial arrangements reveal surprising clues about how ancient Peruvi

entries.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
entries.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. entries.title: Leucine does more than build muscle. It powers up your cells
entries.summary: The essential amino acid leucine can boost cellular energy production by protecting key proteins on mitochondria from being destroyed. The discovery reveals a new connection between nutrition and metabolism that could eventually lead to new approaches for metabolic disorders and cancer.

entries.title: Scientists find new virus behind mysterious tick illness
entries.summary: Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus

entries.title: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
entries.summary: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. entries.title: Scientists discover first new penguin species in more than 100 years
entries.summary: Genetic evidence has revealed a previously unknown gentoo penguin species on the remote Kerguelen Islands and shown that gentoos actually consist of four distinct species. entries.title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
entries.summary: Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. entries.title: A coral reef thought dead for 60 years is teeming with life
entries.summary: More than 60 years after surveys suggested a deep coral reef off Benin was probably dead, scientists have found it alive. entries.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
entries.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. entries.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
entries.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. entries.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
entries.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. entries.title: Tropical trees built homes for ants. Wasps are taking them over
entries.summary: Predatory wasps are hijacking shelters built by tropical trees for their ant defenders, potentially disrupting an ancient partnership that protects the plants from hungry insects. entries.title: Scientists reveal what seven days of fasting does to the human body
entries.summary: Scientists found that prolonged fasting triggers major changes throughout the body, but many of the most interesting effects only appeared after about three days without food. The results suggest fasting may influence health in ways that go beyond weight loss and could eventually inspire treatments

entries.title: Scientists discover a human brain gene that can jump through DNA
entries.summary: Scientists have discovered a human gene with a remarkable double life: it appears to play an important role in brain cells while still retaining the ability to jump around the genome. entries.title: Don’t toss cannabis leaves: They may contain rare compounds with medical potential
entries.summary: Scientists discovered rare flavoalkaloids in Cannabis leaves for the first time, along with dozens of other phenolic compounds that had never been reported in the plant. The findings suggest that Cannabis leaves, often discarded as waste, may contain a surprisingly rich source of potentially useful

entries.title: Scientists discovered two bizarre new sea spiders that are “nightmare fuel”
entries.summary: Scientists discovered two strange new sea spider species in the Salish Sea, including a hairy-legged, red-eyed species that can groom itself with comb-like appendages. entries.title: Scientists discover the first diplodocus ever found outside North America
entries.summary: A 150-million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Spain has been identified as the first confirmed Diplodocus ever found outside North America. The giant sauropod measured about 25 meters long and was preserved well enough for researchers to match distinctive features in its tail bones to the famous genus

entries.title: Scientists just named a new snake after Guns N’ Roses legend Slash
entries.summary: A newly discovered snake from New Guinea has been named after Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash, who has loved reptiles since childhood. Genetic testing and physical differences confirmed that the reddish-brown groundsnake, Lielaphis slashi, is a species scientists had never formally recognized before.

entries.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
entries.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. entries.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
entries.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. entries.title: The secret to longer life may be hidden in bat DNA
entries.summary: Long-lived bats appear to combine powerful immune defenses with unusual strategies for eliminating damaged cells, potentially helping them avoid cancer and disease for decades. Researchers hope these genetic tricks could eventually reveal new ways to protect human health during aging.

entries.title: 66-million-year-old feather in dinosaur poop may reveal why birds survived the asteroid
entries.summary: A feather discovered inside 66-million-year-old fossilized dinosaur poop may help explain why modern birds survived the asteroid catastrophe. entries.title: Wasps are disappearing this summer, and scientists are worried
